title: Rosen Contacted Manhattan Prosecutors After Manafort’s Lawyer Raised Rikers Concerns
description_short: Jeffrey Rosen sought Manhattan prosecutors’ views after Manafort’s lawyer asked that he remain in federal custody over Rikers concerns.
description_medium: NBC News reported that Paul Manafort’s lawyer asked federal officials to keep him in federal custody because of health and safety concerns about Rikers Island. Deputy Attorney General Jeffrey Rosen sent Manhattan prosecutors the lawyer’s letter and asked for their views. Their office said it made no housing recommendation; Manafort stayed in federal custody in Manhattan.
description_long: In June 2019, as Manhattan prosecutors prepared a state case against Paul Manafort, his lawyer asked the Bureau of Prisons to keep him in federal custody, citing health and personal-safety concerns about Rikers Island. NBC News obtained a letter Deputy Attorney General Jeffrey Rosen sent to Manhattan prosecutors with the defense letter attached; Rosen asked whether the office had a response. District Attorney Cyrus Vance replied that his office had made no recommendation about where Manafort should be housed and took no position among Rikers, another city facility, or the Metropolitan Correctional Center. Federal officials ultimately kept Manafort in federal custody at the Manhattan facility while making him available to state prosecutors. The reporting supports DOJ involvement after a defense request, followed by consultation with prosecutors and a stated health-and-safety rationale. It does not establish that DOJ independently ordered Manafort kept out of Rikers, that prosecutors opposed the arrangement, or that President Trump directed the decision. The prior title’s claim of a Trump DOJ order therefore overstates the documented sequence.
date_precision: day; federal officials informed Manhattan prosecutors on Monday, June 17, 2019, as reported by NBC News on June 18.

title: Trump Opposed Postal Funding While Linking It to Mail Voting
description_short: Trump opposed additional Postal Service funding in August 2020 and said it was needed to process ballots for universal mail voting.
description_medium: In August 2020, Donald Trump opposed additional Postal Service funding during COVID-19 relief negotiations and said the money was needed to process ballots for universal mail voting. CNBC reported the remarks and quoted Postmaster General Louis DeJoy rejecting the idea that he would make Postal Service decisions at Trump’s direction. The reporting does not substantiate the original claim that Trump pressured DeJoy to slow delivery.
description_long: On August 13, 2020, President Donald Trump opposed additional funding for the U.S. Postal Service during negotiations over coronavirus relief. In a Fox Business interview, he said the Postal Service needed money to process “all of these millions and millions of ballots” and said that without a deal it could not have universal mail-in voting. CNBC reported those remarks and quoted Postmaster General Louis DeJoy saying the idea that he would make Postal Service decisions at Trump’s direction was “wholly off-base.” The reporting supports Trump’s public funding position and the connection he expressly made between postal resources and mail voting. It does not establish that Trump personally directed DeJoy to slow mail delivery. The supplied research notes also distinguish Trump’s opposition to funding from DeJoy’s separate operational changes and report that Trump said he did not know what DeJoy was doing. This record should describe the funding dispute and statement, not assert an unproven instruction to reduce delivery service, voter-suppression intent, or resulting postal harm. No enacted funding decision or measured effect is established by the cited article.
